labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Simple Pendulum
labs.aim: Measure the time period of a simple pendulum, study how it depends on length, and find g from the L–T² graph.
labs.formula: T = 2π √(L / g)     g = 4π² L / T²
procedure: Set the effective length L with the slider.
Drag the bob sideways (keep amplitude small) or tap “Release bob”.
The stopwatch starts as the bob first passes the mean position.
After at least 10 oscillations tap “Record reading”.
Repeat for 5–6 lengths. The L–T² graph is a straight line.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Hooke's Law — Spring Constant
labs.aim: Verify Hooke’s law and find the spring constant of a helical spring from its load–extension graph.
apparatus: Slotted masses with hanger (50 g each)
labs.formula: F = k x     k = F / x = mg / x
procedure: Note the pointer position with no load (zero).
Add slotted masses in steps of 50 g.
Wait until the spring comes to rest and read the extension.
Tap “Record reading” for each load.
Plot F against x; the slope gives k.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Friction on an Inclined Plane
labs.aim: Find the angle of repose and the coefficient of static friction between a block and different surfaces.
labs.formula: Block slides when tan θ > μs      μs = tan θ(repose)
procedure: Choose a surface and keep the plane horizontal.
Increase the angle slowly, 1° at a time.
Record a reading at each angle: does the block stay or slide?
The smallest angle at which it slides is the angle of repose.
Repeat for other surfaces and compare.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Archimedes' Principle
labs.aim: Show that the loss in weight of a solid immersed in a liquid equals the weight of the liquid it displaces.
labs.formula: Loss of weight = Buoyant force = ρ(liquid) · V(immersed) · g
procedure: Hang the solid from the spring balance and note its weight in air.
Fill the overflow can up to the spout.
Lower the solid gradually into the liquid.
At each step read the balance and the displaced liquid in the cylinder.
Compare loss of weight with weight of displaced liquid.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Vernier Callipers
labs.aim: Use Vernier callipers to measure the diameter of a small spherical or cylindrical body.
labs.formula: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 0.1 mm     D = MSR + (VSC × LC)
procedure: Close the jaws with nothing between them and check for zero error.
Place the object and slide the movable jaw until it grips the object.
Read the main scale just before the vernier zero (MSR).
Find the vernier division that coincides with a main scale mark (VSC).
Record; repeat 3 times and take the mean.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Resonance Tube — Speed of Sound
labs.aim: Find the speed of sound in air at room temperature using a resonance tube and two resonance positions.
labs.formula: l₂ − l₁ = λ/2     v = 2 f (l₂ − l₁)
procedure: Choose a tuning fork and tap “Strike tuning fork” (turn sound on to hear it).
Slowly change the air-column length by moving the water level.
Find the position of loudest sound (first resonance l₁) and record.
Increase the length to find the second resonance l₂ and record.
Speed of sound v = 2f(l₂ − l₁). Repeat with another fork.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Screw Gauge
labs.aim: Use a screw gauge to measure the diameter of a wire and the thickness of a sheet, correcting for zero error.
labs.formula:
LC = pitch ÷ circular divisions = 0.5 ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm
Reading = PSR + (CSR × LC)
Corrected = Observed − Zero error
procedure: Close the gauge with nothing between the studs (Object: None) and note the zero error.
Place the object and turn the thimble (drag it, or use − / +) until the spindle just touches it.
Read the pitch scale (PSR) visible on the sleeve.
Read the circular-scale division (CSR) on the reference line.
Record; subtract the zero error to get the corrected reading.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Parallelogram Law of Vectors
labs.aim: Verify the parallelogram law of vector addition with Gravesand’s apparatus.
labs.formula:
R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ)
The diagonal of the parallelogram on P and Q equals R and points vertically up.
procedure: Hang weights P and Q over the pulleys and R at the central knot.
Let the knot come to rest; mark the directions of the three threads.
Draw OA = P and OB = Q to scale along the threads; complete the parallelogram.
Measure the diagonal OC — compare with R (vertically upward).
Record and repeat with different weights.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Principle of Moments — Mass of a Body
labs.aim: Find the mass of a given body using a metre scale balanced on a knife edge (principle of moments).
labs.formula:
Anticlockwise moment = Clockwise moment
M × d₁ = m × d₂     →     m = M d₁ / d₂
procedure: Balance the metre scale at its 50 cm mark on the knife edge.
Hang the known mass on the left and the unknown body on the right.
Slide them (drag) until the scale is horizontal again.
Record d₁ and d₂ measured from the fulcrum.
Repeat for 3 positions; find the mean mass.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Boyle's Law
labs.aim: Study how the pressure of a fixed mass of air varies with its volume at constant temperature and plot P against 1/V.
labs.formula: P = P₀ + h      P × V = constant      (V ∝ l in a uniform tube)
procedure: Note the atmospheric pressure P₀ from the barometer.
Raise or lower the open tube (drag it) and wait for the mercury to settle.
Read the difference in mercury levels h (+ if open side is higher) and the air column l.
Record 6–8 readings above and below the starting level.
Plot P against 1/l — a straight line shows P ∝ 1/V.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Surface Tension — Capillary Rise
labs.aim: Determine the surface tension of water (and other liquids) by the capillary rise method.
labs.formula: T = r h ρ g / 2      (contact angle ≈ 0°)      h ∝ 1/r
procedure: Dip clean capillary tubes vertically into the liquid.
Wait for the liquid to rise and settle.
Measure the height h of the meniscus above the liquid surface in the selected tube.
Record for each tube radius.
Compute T; plot h against 1/r.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Viscosity — Stokes' Law (Terminal Velocity)
labs.aim: Determine the coefficient of viscosity of a liquid by measuring the terminal velocity of steel balls falling through it.
apparatus: Tall glass jar with glycerine / castor oil
Rubber bands as marks A and B (30 cm apart)
labs.formula: v = 2 r² (ρ − σ) g / 9η      η = 2 r² (ρ − σ) g / 9v      (ρ steel = 7800 kg/m³)
procedure: Choose a ball radius and tap “Drop ball”.
The ball reaches terminal velocity before mark A.
The stopwatch runs from mark A to mark B automatically.
Record t; v = 30 cm / t.
Repeat for other radii; plot v against r² and compute η.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Thermometer & Newton's Law of Cooling
labs.aim: Read a laboratory thermometer and study how hot water cools with time; plot the cooling curve.
labs.formula: Rate of cooling ∝ (T − Ts)      T = Ts + (T₀ − Ts) e^(−kt)
procedure: Pour hot water into the calorimeter and place it in the enclosure.
Start the stopwatch.
Read the thermometer at regular intervals (e.g. every minute) and record.
Continue until the temperature falls by about 30 °C.
Plot temperature against time — the cooling curve.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Specific Heat — Method of Mixtures
labs.aim: Determine the specific heat capacity of a solid by the method of mixtures.
labs.formula:
Heat lost by solid = Heat gained by water + calorimeter
m c (T₁ − T) = (M × 4.18 + 60 × 0.385)(T − T₂)
procedure: Choose the metal and the masses of solid and water.
Heat the solid in steam until it reaches 100 °C (T₁).
Note the water temperature T₂ (room temperature).
Drop the solid quickly into the calorimeter, stir, and wait for the final steady temperature T.
Record and compute c.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Newton's Third Law — Two Spring Balances
labs.aim: Verify Newton’s third law of motion using two spring balances pulling on each other.
labs.formula: Force of A on B = − Force of B on A      (action = reaction, opposite in direction)
procedure: Hook balance A to the wall and balance B to A.
Pull B (drag the hand) to different forces.
Read both balances each time.
Try the arrangement where both ends are pulled.
Record and compare.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Liquid Pressure Increases with Depth
labs.aim: Show that pressure in a liquid increases with depth, using water jets from holes at different heights.
apparatus: Plastic bottle with 3 holes at different heights
labs.formula:
P = h ρ g      Jet speed v = √(2 g h)
Range on table R = 2 √(h × H)   (H = height of hole above table)
procedure: Fill the bottle and keep the tap running to hold the level constant.
Remove the tape from the holes (switch).
Observe which jet reaches farthest.
Measure the horizontal range of each jet on the table and record.
Repeat with a different water level.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Uniform & Non-uniform Motion
labs.aim: Measure the distance covered by a toy car in equal time intervals and plot a distance–time graph to tell uniform from non-uniform motion.
apparatus: Toy car on a 2 m track
labs.formula: Speed = distance ÷ time      Uniform motion → straight-line distance–time graph
procedure: Choose the type of motion and tap “Start / pause car”.
A chalk mark appears every second.
Pause and record time and distance at several moments (or record while it runs).
Plot distance against time.
A straight line means uniform motion; a curve means non-uniform.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Laws of Reflection (Plane Mirror)
labs.aim: Verify that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and that incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane.
labs.formula: ∠ i = ∠ r
procedure: Draw the normal at the point where the ray meets the mirror.
Set the angle of incidence (or drag the incident ray).
Observe the reflected ray through the pins.
Measure ∠r with the protractor and record.
Repeat for 5 different angles.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Refraction through a Glass Slab
labs.aim: Trace the path of a ray of light through a rectangular glass slab and measure ∠i, ∠r, ∠e and the lateral shift.
labs.formula: n = sin i / sin r      ∠e = ∠i      d = t sin(i − r) / cos r
procedure: Outline the slab and draw the normal at the entry point.
Choose ∠i (or drag the incident ray).
Look through the slab and fix pins in line with the emergent ray.
Join the points and measure ∠r and ∠e.
Record for 4–5 angles and compute n.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Convex Lens — Image Formation & f
labs.aim: Obtain real images of a candle with a convex lens for different object distances and find its focal length.
labs.formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f      f = uv / (u + v)   (magnitudes)
procedure: Place the lens on the bench and choose u (or drag the candle).
Move the screen (slider or drag) until the image is sharp.
When sharpness > 80 %, tap “Record reading”.
Repeat for 5 object distances beyond F.
Compute f for each; plot 1/u against 1/v.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Concave Mirror — Focal Length
labs.aim: Obtain real images of a candle with a concave mirror for different object distances and find its focal length.
labs.formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f      f = uv / (u + v)   (magnitudes)
procedure: Place the mirror on the bench and choose u (or drag the candle).
Move the screen (slider or drag) until the image is sharp.
When sharpness > 80 %, tap “Record reading”.
Repeat for 5 object distances beyond F.
Compute f for each; plot 1/u against 1/v.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Prism — Angle of Deviation
labs.aim: Trace rays through a glass prism, draw the i–D curve and find the angle of minimum deviation and refractive index.
labs.formula: D = i + e − A      n = sin((A + Dm)/2) / sin(A/2)
procedure: Place the prism and draw the normal on the first face.
Set ∠i (or drag the incident ray) and look for the emergent ray through the other face.
Record ∠e and the deviation D.
Repeat from 30° to 70° in steps of 5°.
Plot i against D and find Dm from the lowest point.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Light, Shadows & Umbra
labs.aim: Show that light travels in straight lines and study how the size of a shadow changes with the position of the object.
labs.formula: Shadow size = object size × (source-to-screen ÷ source-to-object)
procedure: Keep the source and the screen 60 cm apart in a dark room.
Place the ball between them; note the shadow on the screen.
Move the ball closer to the source and record the shadow size.
Move it towards the screen and record again.
Switch to the frosted bulb to see umbra (dark) and penumbra (partial) shadow.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Ohm's Law — V–I Graph
labs.aim: Study the dependence of current (I) on potential difference (V) across a resistor and find its resistance; verify series and parallel combinations.
labs.formula: V = I R      R(series) = R₁ + R₂      1/R(parallel) = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
procedure: Close the plug key (tap it on the board).
Adjust the rheostat (drag its slider) to change the current.
Read the ammeter and voltmeter and record.
Take 5–6 readings; plot V against I.
Change to series / parallel combination and repeat.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Metre Bridge — Unknown Resistance
labs.aim: Find the resistance of a given wire using a metre bridge (Wheatstone bridge principle) and hence its resistivity.
procedure: Choose a value R from the resistance box.
Slide the jockey along the wire (drag it) while watching the galvanometer.
Find the null point where the deflection is zero.
Record l; repeat with 3 values of R.
Compute X for each and take the mean.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: P–N Junction Diode Characteristics
labs.aim: Draw the I–V characteristic curves of a p–n junction diode in forward and reverse bias.
labs.formula: Forward: I rises sharply after the knee (~0.6–0.7 V)      Reverse: tiny saturation current (µA)
procedure: Connect the diode in forward bias.
Increase V in small steps with the potential divider.
Record V and I (mA) at each step.
Switch to reverse bias; record V and I (µA).
Plot I against V for both.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Conductors & Insulators
labs.aim: Test which materials allow electric current to pass through them using a simple circuit with a bulb.
labs.formula: Bulb glows → conductor      Bulb does not glow → insulator
procedure: Make the circuit with a gap between the two clips.
Place a material in the gap.
Close the switch (tap it) and watch the bulb.
Record whether the bulb glows.
Repeat for all materials and classify them.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Magnetic Field Lines of a Bar Magnet
labs.aim: Map the magnetic field around a bar magnet (and pairs of magnets) using a compass and iron filings.
labs.formula: Field lines leave N and enter S; they never cross. Closer lines → stronger field.
procedure: Place the magnet at the centre of the sheet.
Sprinkle iron filings and tap the board — watch the pattern.
Move the compass (drag on the sheet) and note the needle direction.
Try two magnets with like and unlike poles facing.
Sketch the field lines in your notebook.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Electromagnetic Induction
labs.aim: Show that a changing magnetic field through a coil induces a current, and study how its direction and size depend on motion, pole and number of turns.
labs.formula: e = − N dΦ/dt   (Faraday & Lenz)
procedure: Connect the coil to the galvanometer.
Push the magnet into the coil (drag it) — note the deflection.
Hold it still — note the reading. Pull it out — note the direction.
Move it faster; change the pole facing the coil; change turns.
Record each case.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Sonometer — Frequency & Length
labs.aim: Study how the resonant length of a stretched wire depends on frequency (law of length) and on tension.
labs.formula: f = (1 / 2l) √(T / μ)      f × l = constant (T fixed)      l ∝ √T (f fixed)
procedure: Hang a load to set the tension; place the paper rider in the middle of the wire.
Tap “Strike fork & place on box”.
Move the bridge (drag it) until the rider flutters and falls — resonance.
Record l; repeat for each tuning fork, then for other loads.
Check f × l is constant; plot l against 1/f.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Speed of a Pulse in a Slinky
labs.aim: Determine the speed of a pulse travelling along a stretched slinky.
labs.formula: v = distance ÷ time = (number of trips × L) ÷ t
procedure: Stretch the slinky to length L; the far end is held fixed.
Tap “Send pulse” — a sharp jerk at the free end.
The stopwatch counts trips as the pulse reflects back and forth.
After a few trips, record the trips and the time.
Repeat for other lengths and pulse types.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Laws of Reflection of Sound
labs.aim: Verify that sound reflects from a hard surface with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence.
labs.formula: ∠ i = ∠ r      (incident sound, normal and reflected sound in one plane)
procedure: Fix tube 1 at an angle ∠i to the normal with the clock at its end.
Listen through tube 2 and turn it (drag) until the ticking is loudest.
Read ∠r from the protractor.
Record; repeat for other angles of incidence.
Compare ∠i and ∠r.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Sound on an Oscilloscope — Pitch & Loudness
labs.aim: Display sound waves on a CRO; relate frequency to pitch, amplitude to loudness, and measure the time period.
labs.formula: f = 1 / T      T = (divisions per cycle) × (time-base ms/div)
procedure: Set a frequency and amplitude; switch on sound to hear it.
Count the horizontal divisions for one complete wave on the CRO.
T = divisions × time-base; f = 1/T.
Raise the frequency — waves crowd together and the pitch rises.
Raise the amplitude — waves grow taller and the sound is louder.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Pinhole Camera
labs.aim: Make a pinhole camera and study the image of a candle: its nature and how its size changes.
apparatus: Box with a pinhole at one end
Tracing-paper screen at the other end
labs.formula: Image height ÷ Object height = Box length ÷ Object distance
procedure: Light the candle in a dark room and point the pinhole at it.
Look at the image on the tracing-paper screen.
Move the candle closer / farther and note the image size.
Change the box length and the size of the hole.
Record the image height each time.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Refractive Index — Travelling Microscope
labs.aim: Find the refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope (real depth ÷ apparent depth).
labs.formula: n = real depth ÷ apparent depth = (R₃ − R₁) ÷ (R₃ − R₂)
procedure: With no slab, focus the microscope on the cross mark — R₁.
Place the slab over the mark; raise the microscope until the mark is sharp again — R₂.
Focus on the powder on top of the slab — R₃.
Record each reading when the eyepiece image is sharp.
n = (R₃ − R₁)/(R₃ − R₂).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Potentiometer — Compare EMFs & Internal Resistance
labs.aim: Compare the EMFs of two primary cells, and find the internal resistance of a cell, using a potentiometer.
labs.formula: E₁ / E₂ = l₁ / l₂      r = R (l₁ − l₂) / l₂
procedure: Keep the rheostat fixed throughout so the potential gradient stays the same.
Choose a cell; slide the jockey (drag it on the wires) until the galvanometer reads zero.
Record balancing lengths for Leclanché (l₁) and Daniell (l₂) → E₁/E₂.
Connect a shunt R across the Leclanché cell and find the new length.
Compute r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂ for each R.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Galvanometer — Half-deflection Method
labs.aim: Find the resistance of a galvanometer by the half-deflection method and its figure of merit.
labs.formula: G = R S / (R − S)      Figure of merit k = E / ((R + G) θ)
procedure: With K₂ open, set R for a large deflection θ (note it).
Close K₂ (tap it) and adjust the shunt S until the deflection becomes θ/2.
Record R, θ and S.
Repeat for 3–4 values of R.
Compute G and the figure of merit k.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Zener Diode — Reverse Breakdown
labs.aim: Draw the reverse-bias I–V characteristic of a Zener diode and find its breakdown voltage.
apparatus: DC supply 0–10 V with potential divider
labs.formula: Below Vz: almost no current      At Vz: current rises sharply, voltage stays ≈ Vz
procedure: Connect the Zener in reverse bias with the 200 Ω resistor.
Increase the supply in small steps (drag the divider slider).
Record V across the diode and the current I at each step.
Note where the current suddenly rises — the breakdown voltage.
Plot I against V.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Electromagnet
labs.aim: Make an electromagnet and study how its strength depends on the current, the number of turns and the core.
labs.formula: Strength ∝ current × number of turns (much stronger with an iron core)
procedure: Wind the wire on the nail and connect it to the cells through the switch.
Close the switch (tap it) and watch the pins below.
Count the pins lifted; open the switch and watch them drop.
Change cells, turns and core; record each time.
Compare the strengths.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Projectile Motion — Range & Angle
labs.aim: Launch a projectile at different angles with the same speed; find the angle of maximum range and verify R = u² sin 2θ / g.
labs.formula: R = u² sin 2θ / g      H = u² sin² θ / 2g      T = 2u sin θ / g
procedure: Set the launch speed u.
Set the launch angle θ.
Tap “Launch” and let the ball land.
Record θ, range R and maximum height H.
Repeat for 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°. Complementary angles give the same range.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Uniform Circular Motion — Centripetal Force
labs.aim: Measure the centripetal force needed to keep a body in a circle and verify F = m v² / r.
labs.formula: F = m v² / r = m ω² r      v = 2π r / T
procedure: Choose the mass m and radius r.
Set the speed v.
Read the string tension F on the force sensor.
Record and repeat for several speeds.
Plot F against v²; slope = m / r. Tap “Cut the string” to see the direction the body leaves.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Collisions — Conservation of Momentum
labs.aim: Study elastic and perfectly inelastic collisions of two gliders on an air track; show that total momentum is conserved while kinetic energy may not be.
labs.formula: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂      Elastic: KE conserved      Perfectly inelastic: v = m₁u₁ / (m₁ + m₂)
procedure: Choose the masses and the type of collision.
Set the speed of glider A (B starts at rest).
Tap “Launch”.
After the collision, record the velocities.
Compare total momentum and kinetic energy before and after.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Spring–Mass Oscillator (SHM)
labs.aim: Study simple harmonic motion of a mass on a spring; show that T² ∝ m and find the spring constant k.
labs.formula: T = 2π √(m / k)      T² = (4π² / k) m      x = A sin(ωt)
procedure: Choose the spring and the mass.
Tap “Pull & release”. The stopwatch counts 10 oscillations.
Record when 10 oscillations are complete.
Repeat for 4–5 masses.
Plot T² against m; k = 4π² / slope.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Doppler Effect in Sound
labs.aim: Observe how the frequency heard by a stationary listener changes when a sound source moves towards or away from them.
labs.formula: Source approaching: f′ = f v / (v − vₛ)      Source receding: f′ = f v / (v + vₛ)      v (sound) = 340 m/s
procedure: Choose the source frequency f.
Set the source speed vₛ and direction.
Watch the wavefronts bunch up in front and spread out behind.
Read f′ on the counter and record.
Repeat for several speeds.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Coulomb's Law — Force Between Charges
labs.aim: Measure the electrostatic force between two point charges and show that F ∝ q₁q₂ and F ∝ 1/r².
labs.formula: F = k q₁ q₂ / r²      k = 1 / (4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²
procedure: Choose the charges q₁ and q₂ (sign included).
Set the separation r.
Read the force and its direction (attraction or repulsion).
Record for 5–6 separations.
Plot F against 1/r²; the line passes through the origin.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Charging & Discharging a Capacitor (RC)
labs.aim: Record the voltage across a capacitor while it charges through a resistor and find the time constant τ = RC.
labs.formula: Charging: V = E (1 − e^(−t/RC))      Discharging: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC)      τ = RC (V reaches 63 % of E)
procedure: Choose R and C. Note τ = RC.
Tap “Charge” — the stopwatch starts.
Record V every few seconds.
After about 5τ, tap “Discharge” and record again.
Plot V against t; read τ where V = 0.63 E.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Photoelectric Effect — Planck’s Constant
labs.aim: Find the stopping potential for light of different frequencies; determine Planck’s constant and the work function of the metal.
labs.formula: h f = φ + e V₀      V₀ = (h / e) f − φ / e      f = c / λ
procedure: Choose the metal and the wavelength λ.
Increase the retarding voltage until the photocurrent just becomes zero.
Record this stopping potential V₀.
Repeat for 4–5 wavelengths. Change intensity: V₀ does not change.
Plot V₀ against f: slope = h/e, x-intercept = threshold frequency.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Radioactive Decay — Half-life
labs.aim: Watch a sample of unstable nuclei decay at random; record the number left with time and find the half-life.
labs.formula: N = N₀ e^(−λt)      T½ = ln 2 / λ = 0.693 / λ
procedure: Choose the isotope (half-life).
Tap “Start”. Each nucleus decays at random.
Record N at regular time intervals.
Plot N against t (curve) — or ln N against t (straight line).
Find the time for N to halve. Reset and repeat: each run differs slightly — decay is random.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Series LCR Circuit — Resonance
labs.aim: Vary the frequency of an AC source in a series LCR circuit, plot current against frequency and find the resonant frequency.
labs.formula: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)      X_L = 2πfL      X_C = 1 / (2πfC)      f₀ = 1 / (2π√(LC))
procedure: Choose C and R.
Vary the frequency f in steps.
Record the current at each frequency.
Plot I against f; the peak is at resonance f₀.
Compare with 1/(2π√LC). A larger R makes the peak flatter (lower Q).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Newton's Second Law — F = ma
labs.aim: Pull a trolley with different hanging weights, measure its acceleration and show that a ∝ F (mass fixed), i.e. F = ma.
apparatus: Two light gates 1 m apart / stopwatch
labs.formula: F = m a      a = 2s / t²      1 N = 1 kg·m/s²   ·   1 dyne = 1 g·cm/s² = 10⁻⁵ N
procedure: Choose the trolley mass.
Choose the hanging mass — its weight is the pulling force F.
Tap “Release” and time the trolley over 1 m.
Record t; a = 2s/t² is calculated.
Repeat for 5 forces and plot F against a. Slope = total mass.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Inertia — Passenger in a Braking Bus
labs.aim: See why a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes: the body tends to continue its motion (Newton’s first law). Find the braking rate at which a block on the floor starts to slide.
labs.formula: Block stays with the bus if a ≤ μ g      Block slides forward if a > μ g      (no forward force acts on it!)
procedure: Choose the floor surface (μ).
Set the braking deceleration a.
Tap “Drive & brake”.
Record whether the block slides forward.
Find the smallest a at which it slides; compare with μg. Try “Start suddenly”: the block slides backward.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Apparent Weight in a Lift
labs.aim: Read a spring balance holding a mass inside a lift that accelerates up, down, moves uniformly or falls freely; relate the reading to R = m(g ± a).
labs.formula: Accelerating up: R = m(g + a)      Accelerating down: R = m(g − a)      Uniform velocity: R = mg      Free fall: R = 0
procedure: Choose the mass m.
Choose the motion of the lift and its acceleration a.
Read the spring balance (apparent weight).
Record and repeat for each motion.
Plot R against a (up = +, down = −); slope = m, intercept = mg.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Fundamental Forces — Gravity vs Electric
labs.aim: Compare the gravitational and electrostatic forces between two particles at the same distance, and see how much stronger the electric force is.
labs.formula: F_g = G m₁m₂ / r²   (G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹)      F_e = k q₁q₂ / r²   (k = 9×10⁹)      Both ∝ 1/r², so F_e / F_g is the same at every distance
procedure: Choose a pair of particles.
Change the separation r (powers of ten).
Read F_g, F_e and their ratio.
Record for 4–5 distances.
Plot log F against log r: slope −2 for both (inverse-square law).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Charging by Rubbing & the Electroscope
labs.aim: Charge objects by rubbing, find the sign of each charge, check that the charge is a whole number of electrons (Q = ne) and that total charge is conserved.
labs.formula: Q = ± n e   (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, n a whole number)      Charge gained by one = charge lost by the other (conservation)
procedure: Choose the pair of materials.
Tap “Rub 10 times”. Electrons move from one material to the other.
Touch the rod to the electroscope — the leaves diverge.
Record the charge on each object.
Rub more: Q grows in steps of e; the two charges are always equal and opposite.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Drift Velocity of Electrons
labs.aim: See electrons drifting slowly through a wire while moving randomly at high speed; relate current to drift velocity: I = n e A v_d.
labs.formula: I = n e A v_d      J = I / A = n e v_d      v_d = e E τ / m      mobility μ = v_d / E
procedure: Choose the material and the wire thickness.
Set the current I.
Watch the slow drift (orange) against the fast random motion.
Read v_d and record.
Plot v_d against I: straight line. Thicker wire → smaller v_d for the same I.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Resistance of a Wire — Length, Area, Material, Temperature
labs.aim: Measure how the resistance of a wire depends on its length, thickness, material and temperature, and find the resistivity ρ.
apparatus: Wires of constantan, nichrome and copper
labs.formula: R = ρ L / A      A = π d² / 4      R_T = R₀ (1 + α ΔT)      Stretched to n× length (same volume): R → n² R
procedure: Choose the material and the diameter.
Set the length L with the jockey.
Read R and record. Repeat for 5 lengths — R ∝ L.
Change the diameter: R ∝ 1/d².
Heat the wire: R rises for metals (almost none for constantan). Try “Stretch 2×”.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Resistors in Series & Parallel — Voltage and Current Division
labs.aim: Connect three resistors in series or in parallel; measure the voltage across and current through each and verify the combination rules.
labs.formula: Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, same I, V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃, Vᵢ = I Rᵢ      Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃, same V, I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃, Iᵢ = V / Rᵢ
procedure: Choose the three resistors.
Choose series or parallel.
Read the total current and every voltage / branch current.
Record.
Check: series voltages add up to 12 V; parallel currents add up to the total.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Kirchhoff's Laws — Two-loop Circuit
labs.aim: Measure the currents in a two-source network and verify Kirchhoff's junction law (ΣI = 0) and loop law (ΣE = ΣIR).
labs.formula: Junction law: I₁ + I₂ = I₃   (charge conservation)      Loop law: E₁ − I₁R₁ − I₃R₃ = 0,  E₂ − I₂R₂ − I₃R₃ = 0   (energy conservation)
procedure: Set E₁, E₂ and the three resistors.
Read I₁, I₂ and I₃ (a negative value means opposite to the arrow).
Record.
Check I₁ + I₂ − I₃ = 0 at the junction.
Check the sum of EMFs equals the sum of IR drops in each loop.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Joule's Law of Heating — H = I²Rt
labs.aim: Heat water with a resistance coil and show that the heat produced is proportional to I² (for fixed R and t).
apparatus: Calorimeter with 200 g water and stirrer
labs.formula: H = I² R t  (joules)      H = (m c + C_cal) ΔT      P = I²R = V²/R      1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
procedure: Choose R and set the current I.
Tap “Switch on”. The clock runs 10× faster.
After 2 minutes (120 s) record the temperature rise ΔT.
Cool the water (“New water”) and repeat for other currents.
Plot ΔT against I²: a straight line → H ∝ I².

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Electric Bulbs in Series & Parallel
labs.aim: Connect two bulbs of different power ratings to the 220 V mains in series and in parallel; compare their brightness (actual power).
apparatus: Bulbs rated 40 W, 60 W and 100 W at 220 V
labs.formula: R = V_rated² / P_rated   (R₄₀W > R₁₀₀W)      Series: same I → P = I²R → higher-R (lower-watt) bulb glows brighter      Parallel: same V → each gives its rated power
procedure: Choose the ratings of bulbs A and B.
Choose series or parallel.
Compare the glow and read each bulb’s actual power.
Record.
Explain: in series the 40 W bulb is brighter than the 100 W bulb!

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Household Circuit — Power, Fuse & Energy Bill
labs.aim: Switch on appliances in a domestic parallel circuit, find the current drawn, see when the fuse blows, and calculate energy used in kWh.
apparatus: 220 V mains with live, neutral and earth
Appliances: bulb, fan, TV, iron, heater
labs.formula: I = P / V      Fuse blows if I > rated current      Energy (kWh) = P(kW) × t(h)      1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
procedure: Choose the fuse rating.
Switch appliances on one by one; watch the total current.
Find the combination that blows the fuse (overloading).
Set hours of use per day and read the units consumed and the cost.
Record. Try “Short circuit” — the fuse protects the wiring.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Magnetic Field of a Straight Wire & a Circular Loop
labs.aim: Measure the magnetic field produced by a current in a long straight wire, at the centre of a circular coil, and on its axis (Biot–Savart law).
labs.formula: Straight wire: B = μ₀ I / (2π r)      Coil centre: B = μ₀ N I / (2R)      Coil axis: B = μ₀ N I R² / [2 (R² + x²)^(3/2)]      μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A
procedure: Choose the conductor.
Set the current I.
Set the distance d (r from wire / R of coil / x along axis).
Read B and record.
For the wire, plot B against 1/r — a straight line. Reverse I: the compass reverses.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Force on a Current-carrying Conductor
labs.aim: Measure the force on a wire carrying current in a magnetic field (F = BIL sin θ), find its direction by Fleming’s left-hand rule, and measure the force between two parallel currents.
labs.formula: Wire in field: F = B I L sin θ   (Fleming’s left-hand rule)      Parallel wires: F / L = μ₀ I₁ I₂ / (2π d) — like currents attract, unlike repel
procedure: Choose the arrangement.
Set the current (and B, θ or the second current and spacing).
Read the force on the balance.
Record for 5 currents — F ∝ I.
Reverse the current: the force reverses. For parallel wires, reverse one current: attraction becomes repulsion.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field
labs.aim: Fire charged particles into a uniform magnetic field; measure the radius of the circular path and the time period, and see helical motion when entering at an angle.
apparatus: Uniform magnetic field region (into the page)
labs.formula: r = m v sinθ / (q B)      T = 2π m / (q B)  (independent of speed!)      pitch p = 2π m v cosθ / (q B)      F = q v B sinθ ⟂ v → no work done
procedure: Choose the particle.
Set the speed v and the field B.
Fire at θ = 90°: the track is a circle — read r and T.
Record for 4–5 speeds; plot r against v.
Set θ < 90°: the path becomes a helix; read the pitch.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Magnetic Flux & the AC Generator (Faraday’s Law)
labs.aim: Rotate a coil in a magnetic field; watch the flux ϕ = NBA cos ωt change and the induced EMF e = NBAω sin ωt appear. Measure how the peak EMF depends on speed.
labs.formula: ϕ = N B A cos θ   (θ = ωt)      e = − dϕ/dt = N B A ω sin ωt      e₀ = N B A ω = 2π f N B A
procedure: Choose the number of turns N, field B and coil area A.
Set the rotation frequency f.
Watch the ϕ – t and e – t graphs: e is maximum when ϕ is zero.
Record the peak EMF e₀.
Repeat for 4–5 speeds and plot e₀ against f.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation — Cavendish Balance
labs.aim: Measure the tiny attraction between lead spheres with a torsion balance; show F ∝ 1/r² and find the universal constant G.
labs.formula: F = G M m / r²      G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²   [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]      Gravity is always attractive, acts along the line joining the masses
procedure: Choose the large mass M (small mass m = 0.73 kg).
Set the centre-to-centre distance r.
Read the force from the deflection of the light spot.
Record for 5 distances.
Plot F against 1/r²; G = slope / (M m).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Variation of g — Height, Depth & Latitude
labs.aim: Find how the acceleration due to gravity changes as you go up from, or down into, the Earth, and with latitude because of Earth’s rotation.
apparatus: Spring balance with a 60 kg person
labs.formula: g = G M / R² ≈ 9.8 m/s²      Height: g_h = g R² / (R + h)² ≈ g (1 − 2h/R)      Depth: g_d = g (1 − d/R)  (zero at the centre)      Latitude: g_λ = g − ω² R cos² λ
procedure: Choose height or depth.
Move the person up or down with the slider.
Read g and the person’s weight.
Record for several values; plot g against the distance.
Compare: g falls with both height and depth; it is greatest at the poles.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Gravitational Field & Potential — Shell and Solid Sphere
labs.aim: Plot the gravitational field E and potential V around a hollow shell and a solid sphere as you move from the centre to far outside.
apparatus: Spherical shell / solid sphere of mass M, radius R
labs.formula: Outside (r ≥ R): E = GM/r², V = −GM/r      Shell inside: E = 0, V = −GM/R (constant)      Solid inside: E = GMr/R³, V = −GM(3R² − r²)/(2R³)      V(∞) = 0
procedure: Choose shell or solid sphere.
Move the probe with the r/R slider.
Read E and V (in units of GM/R² and GM/R).
Record from the centre to 4R.
Note: inside a shell E = 0 but V is NOT zero; V is most negative at the centre of a solid sphere (−1.5 GM/R).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Satellites — Orbital & Escape Velocity
labs.aim: Launch a satellite horizontally at different speeds and heights: see it fall back, orbit in a circle, go into an ellipse, or escape. Measure orbital speed, period and energies.
labs.formula: v₀ = √(GM/r) = √(gR²/r)  (≈ 7.9 km/s near the surface)      T = 2π r / v₀      KE = GMm/2r,  PE = −GMm/r,  TE = −GMm/2r = PE/2      vₑ = √(2GM/R) ≈ 11.2 km/s
procedure: Set the height h of the launch point.
Set the launch speed as a multiple of the circular speed v₀.
Tap “Launch”.
At 1.0 × v₀ the orbit is a circle — record h, v₀ and T.
Try < 1 (falls back / ellipse inside), between 1 and 1.41 (ellipse) and ≥ 1.41 (escapes: v ≥ √2 v₀).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
labs.aim: Watch a planet on an elliptical orbit: verify equal areas in equal times (2nd law) and T² ∝ a³ (3rd law).
labs.formula: 1st law: orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus      2nd law: equal areas in equal times (dA/dt = L/2m = constant)      3rd law: T² ∝ a³  (T in years, a in AU: T² = a³)
procedure: Set the semi-major axis a and the eccentricity e.
Watch the coloured sectors: each is swept in the same time interval.
Note the planet is fastest at perihelion, slowest at aphelion.
Record a and T for 4–5 orbits.
Plot T² against a³: a straight line of slope 1.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Temperature Scales & Thermometry
labs.aim: Read one temperature on the Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin and Reaumur scales and on a scale you design yourself from two fixed points; find the general conversion rule.
apparatus: Custom scale with your own fixed points
procedure: Set the temperature with the slider.
Read all four thermometers.
Set the lower and upper fixed points of your own scale X.
Record readings at 5 temperatures.
Plot F against C: slope 1.8, intercept 32. Find where C = F.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Linear Expansion of a Metal Rod
labs.aim: Heat metal rods in a steam jacket, measure the increase in length with a dial gauge and find the coefficient of linear expansion α (and β, γ).
apparatus: Metal rods (L₀ = 50 cm): aluminium, brass, copper, steel
labs.formula: ΔL = α L₀ ΔT      α = ΔL / (L₀ ΔT)      β = 2α (area)      γ = 3α (volume)      ρ′ = ρ / (1 + γ ΔT)
procedure: Choose the rod.
Raise the temperature with the steam control.
Read ΔL on the dial gauge.
Record at 5 temperatures.
Plot ΔL against ΔT; α = slope / L₀. Compare the metals.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Bimetallic Strip & Thermostat
labs.aim: Heat a bimetallic strip and measure how it bends; find the radius of the arc and use the strip as a thermostat switch.
apparatus: Brass–invar steel / aluminium–steel bimetallic strip (10 cm, each layer 0.5 mm)
labs.formula: Radius of the bent strip: R = d / [(α₁ − α₂) ΔT]   (d = thickness of each strip)      Tip deflection y ≈ L² / (2R)      Heated: brass (higher α) on the outside (convex side); cooled: brass on the inside
procedure: Choose the pair of metals.
Raise or lower the temperature.
Read R and the tip deflection y.
Record at 5 temperatures; y ∝ ΔT.
Set the contact gap: the bulb switches off when the strip touches — a thermostat.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Distance vs Displacement
labs.aim: Move along different paths and compare the distance travelled (scalar, path length) with the displacement (vector, shortest straight line from start to finish).
labs.formula: Distance = total path length (≥ 0, never decreases)      Displacement = change in position (has direction; can be zero)      |displacement| ≤ distance
procedure: Choose the path.
Move along it with the “Progress” slider.
Compare distance and displacement (arrow).
Record at several points: half-way, full circle etc.
Note: after one full lap the displacement is zero but the distance is 2πR.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Average Speed — Equal Distances vs Equal Times
labs.aim: A car covers a journey in two parts at different speeds. Find its average speed when the parts are equal in distance and when they are equal in time.
labs.formula: Average speed = total distance / total time      Equal distances: v = 2v₁v₂ / (v₁ + v₂)  (harmonic mean)      Equal times: v = (v₁ + v₂) / 2  (arithmetic mean)
procedure: Choose “equal distances” or “equal times”.
Set the two speeds v₁ and v₂.
Tap “Drive” and read the total time.
Record the average speed.
Compare: with equal distances the average is less than (v₁ + v₂)/2 — the car spends longer at the lower speed.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Equations of Motion & Motion Graphs
labs.aim: Drive a car with constant acceleration, watch its x–t and v–t graphs build up, and verify v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
apparatus: Car on a straight road with position sensor
labs.formula: v = u + a t      s = u t + ½ a t²      v² = u² + 2 a s      slope of v–t = a,  area under v–t = displacement
procedure: Set the initial velocity u and acceleration a (negative a = retardation).
Tap “Start”. Pause at any moment.
Record t, v and s.
Repeat at 4–5 times.
Plot v against t: slope = a, intercept = u. Check the three equations in the table.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Stopping Distance — Reaction & Braking
labs.aim: Find the total stopping distance of a car: the distance covered during the driver’s reaction time plus the braking distance (third equation of motion).
labs.formula: Reaction distance = u × t_r      Braking distance = u² / (2a)   (from v² = u² − 2as with v = 0)      Doubling the speed → 4× braking distance
procedure: Set the speed, the driver’s reaction time and the road surface.
Tap “Obstacle!”.
Read the reaction distance, braking distance and total.
Record for 5 speeds.
Plot stopping distance against speed — a curve (∝ u²), not a straight line.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Motion under Gravity — Ball Thrown Upward
labs.aim: Throw a ball straight up; follow its velocity and height, find the maximum height and time of flight, and show that the acceleration is g downward all the time (even at the top).
labs.formula: v = u − g t      h = u t − ½ g t²      H_max = u² / 2g      t_up = u / g      T = 2u / g      At the top: v = 0 but a = g
procedure: Set the launch speed u.
Tap “Throw”. Pause (“Start / pause”) at several moments.
Record t, h and v (+ up, − down).
Plot v against t: a straight line of slope −g.
Note H_max and the total time; the ball returns with the same speed.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Rest, Motion & Relative Velocity
labs.aim: Watch two objects from the ground and from a moving frame: rest and motion depend on the observer. Find the relative velocity and when one catches or meets the other.
apparatus: Two vehicles A and B on a straight road
Observer on the ground / riding with A
labs.formula: v_BA = v_B − v_A   (velocity of B as seen from A)      Meeting / catching time t = initial separation / |relative speed of approach|      In A’s own frame, A is at rest
procedure: Set the velocities of A and B (+ right, − left) and their separation.
Choose the frame: ground or riding with A.
Tap “Go” and watch.
Record v_BA and the meeting time.
Switch frames: the meeting time is the same in both — only the description of motion changes.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Free Fall — Bouncing Ball & Two Bodies Meeting
labs.aim: Drop a ball and follow its successive rebounds; then drop one ball from height H while throwing another up from the ground and find where and when they meet.
apparatus: Balls of different bounciness (coefficient of restitution e)
Tower of height H with scale
labs.formula: Dropped from h: t = √(2h/g), v = √(2gh)      After a bounce: v′ = e v, h′ = e² h      Meeting: one dropped from H, one thrown up with u → t = H / u, meeting height = H − ½ g t²
procedure: Choose the experiment.
Bounce: set the drop height and the ball (e). Tap “Start” and record the height of each rebound.
Meeting: set H and u. Tap “Start”; record the meeting time and height.
Compare with t = H/u (the relative acceleration is zero!).
If u < √(gH/2)… the second ball falls back before they meet — try it.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Graphical Study of Motion — s–t, v–t, a–t
labs.aim: Play a journey and see its displacement–time, velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs together; read slopes and areas at any instant.
labs.formula: Slope of s–t = velocity      Slope of v–t = acceleration      Area under v–t = displacement      Area under a–t = change in velocity      Stationary: s–t horizontal; uniform v: s–t straight; accelerated: s–t curved
procedure: Choose a journey.
Drag the time cursor (or tap “Play”).
Read v from the slope of s–t, a from the slope of v–t.
Record readings at several times.
Check: area under v–t up to t equals the displacement s.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Horizontal Projection — Cliff & Staircase
labs.aim: Throw a ball horizontally from a height; verify the parabolic path y = g x² / 2u², time of flight √(2h/g) and range u√(2h/g). Then roll a ball down a staircase and predict which step it hits first.
apparatus: Ball launcher at the edge of a cliff / table
labs.formula: x = u t,  y = ½ g t²   →   y = g x² / (2u²)      T = √(2h/g)  (independent of u!)      R = u √(2h/g)      v = √(u² + g²t²),  tan θ = g t / u      Staircase: first step hit n = ⌈2 h u² / (g b²)⌉
procedure: Choose cliff or staircase.
Set the launch speed u and the height h (or the step size).
Tap “Launch”. Strobe images are taken every 0.1 s — equal horizontal gaps, growing vertical gaps.
Record T and R for 4–5 speeds: T stays the same, R ∝ u.
Staircase: compare the predicted step with the one hit.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Magnetic Materials — Dia, Para, Ferro, Domains & Hysteresis
labs.aim: Place samples in a strong non-uniform field to classify them; watch the domains of a ferromagnet line up; trace the B–H hysteresis loop of soft iron and steel.
apparatus: Strong electromagnet with pointed pole pieces
Samples: bismuth, copper, water, aluminium, platinum, iron, nickel, steel
labs.formula: Diamagnetic: weakly repelled (moves to weaker field)      Paramagnetic: weakly attracted      Ferromagnetic: strongly attracted (domains)      Soft iron: low retentivity & coercivity (electromagnets)      Steel: high retentivity & coercivity (permanent magnets)
procedure: Choose a sample and switch the field on.
Note whether it moves towards (attracted) or away (repelled) from the strong field, and how strongly.
Record and classify.
For iron or steel, raise H and watch domains align; then reduce H to zero and reverse it to trace the loop.
Compare the retentivity (B at H = 0) and coercivity (H needed for B = 0) of soft iron and steel.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Properties of a Magnet — Directive, Poles & the Sure Test
labs.aim: Show that a freely suspended magnet points north–south, that attraction is strongest at the poles, that like poles repel, that poles always exist in pairs, and that repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.
labs.formula: Freely suspended magnet → rests along geographic N–S (directive property)      Like poles repel, unlike poles attract      Attraction is strongest at the poles, nil at the middle      Breaking a magnet gives two complete magnets (no isolated pole)      Repulsion is the SURE test of a magnet
procedure: Choose an activity.
Directive: turn the suspended magnet away and release — it returns to N–S.
Filings: see how many filings cling along the length of the magnet.
Sure test: bring the N pole of your magnet to each end of bars X and Y; attraction at both ends means iron, repulsion at one end means magnet.
Break: cut the magnet — each piece has N and S poles.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Making & Destroying Magnets
labs.aim: Magnetise a steel bar by single touch, double touch and the electrical method; count how many pins it lifts; then demagnetise it by heating, hammering or an AC coil.
labs.formula: Single touch: stroke one way with one pole      Double touch: two opposite poles from the middle outwards (stronger)      Electrical: DC through a coil (strongest; pole by right-hand rule)      Demagnetise: heat above the Curie point (770 °C for iron), hammer, drop, or AC in a coil
procedure: Choose the method and stroke / switch on as many times as you like.
Count the pins the bar lifts (strength) and record.
Compare the methods for the same number of strokes.
Choose a demagnetising treatment and apply it.
Record the pins lifted afterwards.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Angles, Radians & the Small-angle Approximation
labs.aim: Measure an angle as arc ÷ radius (radian), convert between degree, radian and revolution, and find how small an angle must be for sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (used for the pendulum, parallax and optics).
labs.formula: θ (rad) = arc length / radius = s / r      π rad = 180°      1 rad ≈ 57.3°      1 rev = 2π rad = 360°      Small angles (in radians!): sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ,  cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2
procedure: Set the angle θ.
Read the arc length s on a circle of radius r; θ = s/r in radians.
Compare θ (rad), sin θ and tan θ.
Record the percentage error of sin θ ≈ θ.
Find the largest angle for which the error stays below 1 % (≈ 14°).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Pythagoras & Trigonometric Ratios — Resolving a Force
labs.aim: Pull a block with a force F at angle θ; read its horizontal and vertical components to discover the six trigonometric ratios, Pythagoras’ theorem and sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
apparatus: Spring balance pulling at an angle
labs.formula: Fx = F cos θ   (adjacent)      Fy = F sin θ   (opposite)      F² = Fx² + Fy²   (Pythagoras)      tan θ = Fy / Fx      sin²θ + cos²θ = 1      cosec = 1/sin,  sec = 1/cos,  cot = 1/tan
procedure: Set the force F and the angle θ.
Read Fx and Fy on the sensors.
Record and check Fx² + Fy² = F².
Note the special angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° and the triplet 3-4-5 (θ ≈ 36.87°).
Watch how cos θ falls and sin θ rises as θ increases from 0° to 90°.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Unit Circle — Quadrants, ASTC & Range of a sin θ + b cos θ
labs.aim: Rotate a radius around the unit circle to see the sign of sin, cos and tan in each quadrant (ASTC), the graphs of sin and cos, and find the maximum of a sin θ + b cos θ = √(a² + b²) — used in AC, SHM and projectiles.
labs.formula: ASTC: Q1 All +, Q2 Sin +, Q3 Tan +, Q4 Cos +      −1 ≤ sin θ, cos θ ≤ 1      sin(90° + θ) = cos θ,  sin(180° − θ) = sin θ      a sin θ + b cos θ = √(a² + b²) sin(θ + φ),  tan φ = b/a   → max √(a² + b²)      sin θ cos θ = ½ sin 2θ (max ½)
procedure: Set the angle θ (0° – 360°).
Read sin θ, cos θ, tan θ and the quadrant; note their signs (ASTC).
Set a and b; read y = a sin θ + b cos θ.
Record y at several angles and find its maximum.
Compare with √(a² + b²) and the angle θ = 90° − φ where it occurs.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Coordinate Geometry & the Straight Line (v = u + at)
labs.aim: Plot points on the Cartesian plane, find distance, mid-point and slope, and see that a straight line y = mx + c is exactly the v–t graph of uniform acceleration (slope = a, intercept = u).
apparatus: Two movable points P and Q
labs.formula: Distance PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]      Mid-point = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)      Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan θ      y = mx + c   ↔   v = at + u      Quadrant signs: I (+,+), II (−,+), III (−,−), IV (+,−)
procedure: Place P and Q with the sliders (or drag them on the board).
Read the quadrant of each point, the distance and the mid-point.
Read the slope m, intercept c and the equation of line PQ.
Record. A line with positive slope rises; zero slope is horizontal; undefined slope is vertical.
Treat x as time and y as velocity: m is acceleration, c is initial velocity.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Differentiation — From Average to Instantaneous Velocity
labs.aim: Shrink the interval Δt on a position–time curve and watch the secant (average velocity) turn into the tangent (instantaneous velocity = ds/dt). Check the standard derivatives and find stationary points.
labs.formula: Average velocity = Δs/Δt (secant slope)      v = ds/dt = lim(Δt→0) Δs/Δt (tangent slope)      d(tⁿ)/dt = n tⁿ⁻¹      d(sin t)/dt = cos t      d(eᵗ)/dt = eᵗ      d(c·f)/dt = c·f′,  d(f+g)/dt = f′ + g′      Stationary point: ds/dt = 0
procedure: Choose the function s(t).
Choose the instant t₀.
Reduce Δt step by step and record the secant slope each time.
Compare the limit with the formula value of ds/dt (tangent slope).
Find t₀ where the slope is zero (stationary point: body momentarily at rest).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Integration — Area under a Graph (Displacement, Impulse, Work)
labs.aim: Fill the area under a graph with N rectangles and watch the sum approach the exact definite integral. Use it to find displacement (v–t), impulse (F–t) and work (F–x).
labs.formula: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim(N→∞) Σ f(xᵢ) Δx  = area under the curve      ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C      Fundamental theorem: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) − F(a)      v–t area = displacement · F–t area = impulse = Δp · F–x area = work
procedure: Choose the physical graph.
Set the limits a and b.
Increase the number of strips N and record the sum each time.
Compare with the exact value from F(b) − F(a).
Note: area below the axis counts as negative (e.g. displacement while moving backward).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Squares, Square Roots & Approximations in Physics
labs.aim: Solve a physics quadratic (a ball thrown up passing a height h) and decide which square root is physical; then use (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx to find how a small change in a quantity changes the result.
apparatus: Ball thrown up with speed u
Pendulum of length L (for the approximation)
labs.formula: h = ut − ½gt²   →   t = [u ± √(u² − 2gh)] / g      Both roots physical: going up and coming down      u² < 2gh: no real root — ball never reaches h      Approximation: (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x;  T ∝ √L → 1 % change in L gives ≈ ½ % change in T
procedure: Mode 1 — set u and the height h.
Read the discriminant u² − 2gh and the two roots t₁, t₂ (up and down).
Record; raise h until the discriminant becomes negative.
Mode 2 — set the percentage change in the pendulum length.
Compare the exact new period with the approximation 1 + ½ x.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Impulse & Momentum — Catching a Ball
labs.aim: Stop a moving ball on different surfaces (or with hands drawn back) and show that the same change in momentum produces a smaller force when the stopping time is longer: F = Δp/Δt. Relate momentum and kinetic energy.
apparatus: Force sensor plate with surfaces: concrete, sand, foam cushion
Fielder’s hands (drawn back or held stiff)
labs.formula: p = m v      Impulse J = F Δt = Δp      F_avg = Δp / Δt      Rebound: Δp = m(v + v′)  (larger!)      K = p² / 2m,  p = √(2mK)
procedure: Set the ball speed and choose the stopping surface.
Choose “stop” or “bounce back”.
Tap “Throw”. Read Δp, the contact time Δt and the average force.
Record for each surface.
Compare: same Δp, longer Δt → smaller force (why fielders draw hands back, why cushions protect eggs).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Recoil, Explosion & Rocket — Conservation of Momentum
labs.aim: Show that internal forces cannot change the total momentum of a system: a gun recoils, an exploding body’s fragments fly apart with equal and opposite momenta, and a rocket is pushed forward by the gases it throws back.
apparatus: Body at rest that splits into two fragments
labs.formula: Total p before = total p after      Gun: m v + M V = 0 → V = −m v / M      Explosion from rest: m₁ v₁ = − m₂ v₂, KE shared in inverse ratio of masses      Rocket thrust F = u (dm/dt),  a = F/M − g
procedure: Choose the system.
Set the masses and speeds.
Tap “Fire” and read the velocities.
Record and check that the total momentum after is zero (or unchanged).
Rocket: increase the exhaust rate and see the thrust and acceleration grow; the mass decreases as fuel burns.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Free-body Diagrams — Contact Forces, Strings & Atwood Machine
labs.aim: Draw free-body diagrams for connected bodies and verify the common acceleration, the contact forces between touching blocks, the tensions in light strings and the Atwood machine results.
apparatus: Three blocks on a smooth table
Force sensors between blocks / in strings
labs.formula: System: a = F_ext / (m₁ + m₂ + m₃)      Contact (push on m₁): N₁₂ = (m₂ + m₃) a,  N₂₃ = m₃ a      String train (pull on m₃): T₁ = m₁ a,  T₂ = (m₁ + m₂) a      Atwood: a = (m₁ − m₂) g / (m₁ + m₂),  T = 2 m₁ m₂ g / (m₁ + m₂),  thrust on pulley = 2T
procedure: Choose the arrangement and set the masses (and the force F).
Read the acceleration and the force at each joint.
Draw the FBD of each block (shown) and check ΣF = ma for each.
Record and repeat for other masses.
Atwood: equal masses give a = 0; T lies between m₂g and m₁g.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Inertial & Non-inertial Frames — Pseudo Force
labs.aim: Hang a bob from the roof of an accelerating truck. Explain its tilt from the ground (inertial frame: T and mg give ma) and from inside the truck (non-inertial frame: add a pseudo force −ma and the bob is in equilibrium). Measure a from the tilt.
apparatus: Truck with accelerometer bob hanging from the roof
Observer on the ground and observer in the truck
labs.formula: Inertial frame: T sin θ = m a,  T cos θ = m g      Non-inertial frame: pseudo force −m a (opposite to the frame’s acceleration) → equilibrium      tan θ = a / g,   T = m √(g² + a²)      Pseudo forces have no reaction pair (Newton’s 3rd law does not apply)
procedure: Set the truck’s acceleration a (negative = braking).
Read the tilt angle θ of the bob.
Switch the observer between the ground and the truck: compare the two FBDs.
Record θ and calculate a = g tan θ.
Note: braking tilts the bob forward; uniform velocity gives no tilt.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Static & Kinetic Friction — Pulling a Block
labs.aim: Pull a block with a spring balance at increasing force: static friction grows to a limiting value, then the block slides and the friction drops to kinetic friction. See how pushing or pulling at an angle changes the normal reaction and the friction.
apparatus: Surfaces: glass, wood, sandpaper, oiled wood
labs.formula: Static: f_s = applied force (self-adjusting) ≤ μ_s N      Limiting friction f_L = μ_s N      Kinetic: f_k = μ_k N   (μ_k < μ_s)      Pull at angle θ above horizontal: N = mg − F sin θ;  push down at θ: N = mg + F sin θ      Rolling friction ≪ sliding friction
procedure: Choose the surface and the mass.
Raise the applied force slowly; watch the friction force follow it.
Note the force at which the block starts sliding (limiting friction) and record it.
After it slides, read the smaller kinetic friction.
Pull at an angle: the normal reaction falls, so friction falls (why pulling a lawn roller is easier than pushing).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines — Rays & Beams
labs.aim: Look at a candle through three cardboards with holes: you see it only when the holes are in one straight line. Identify parallel, convergent and divergent beams, and luminous and non-luminous bodies.
apparatus: Three cardboards with small holes on stands
Torch, lens and mirror for beams
labs.formula: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium (rectilinear propagation)      Ray = path of light;  beam = bundle of rays: parallel, convergent, divergent      Speed of light in vacuum c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s — sunlight takes ≈ 8 min 20 s to reach Earth
procedure: Activity 1: line up the three holes and look at the candle.
Shift the middle cardboard sideways with the slider — the candle disappears.
Record the offset and whether the flame is seen.
Activity 2: choose each type of beam and identify where it comes from.
Note: we see non-luminous bodies only by the light they reflect.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Shadows in Space — Solar & Lunar Eclipses
labs.aim: Move the Moon around the Earth and see when its shadow falls on the Earth (solar eclipse) or the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon (lunar eclipse); identify umbra and penumbra and total, partial and annular eclipses.
labs.formula: Shadow needs: a source, an opaque object, a screen      Umbra: total darkness · Penumbra: partial darkness      Solar eclipse: Sun – Moon – Earth in a line (new-moon day)      Lunar eclipse: Sun – Earth – Moon in a line (full-moon day)      Annular: Moon too far — its umbra does not reach Earth
procedure: Move the Moon around its orbit with the slider.
Find the position where the Moon’s shadow reaches the Earth.
Change the Moon’s distance: near → total, far → annular.
Find the position where the Moon enters the Earth’s shadow.
Record the type of eclipse at each position.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Plane Mirror — Image, Lateral Inversion, Rotation & Image Speed
labs.aim: Study the image formed by a plane mirror: as far behind as the object is in front, same size, virtual and laterally inverted. See regular vs diffuse reflection, that rotating the mirror by θ turns the reflected ray by 2θ, and how fast the image moves.
labs.formula: Image distance = object distance (behind the mirror)      Image: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted      Mirror rotated by θ → reflected ray turns by 2θ      Deviation δ = 180° − 2i      Object moves at v towards mirror → image moves at v towards mirror; relative speed of approach = 2v      Smallest mirror to see full height = half the height
procedure: Choose the activity.
Image: move the object; compare object and image distances and look at the letter F.
Rotate: turn the mirror by θ and measure the turn of the reflected ray.
Speed: move the object towards the mirror and compare speeds.
Surface: compare a polished and a rough surface.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Two Plane Mirrors — Number of Images & Periscope
labs.aim: Place an object between two plane mirrors inclined at angle θ and count the images; find the rule n = 360°/θ − 1. Build a periscope from two mirrors at 45°.
labs.formula: m = 360° / θ      m even → n = m − 1      m odd: object on the bisector → n = m − 1, otherwise n = m      Parallel mirrors (θ = 0) → infinite images      Periscope: two mirrors parallel, each at 45°, deviation 90° + 90°
procedure: Choose “angled mirrors”.
Set the angle θ; count the images (drawn on the circle).
Record θ and the number of images; compare with 360/θ − 1.
Move the object off the bisector for odd m.
Choose “periscope” to see how light is turned twice by 90°.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Spherical Mirrors — Ray Diagrams, Mirror Formula & Magnification
labs.aim: Draw the image formed by a concave or convex mirror for any object position using principal rays; verify 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and m = −v/u with the New Cartesian sign convention.
apparatus: Object arrow on an optical bench
labs.formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f      f = R/2      m = h′/h = −v/u      Sign convention: distances measured from the pole; along the incident light +, against it −; upward +, downward −      Concave f < 0, convex f > 0      Real images: v < 0 (in front); virtual: v > 0 (behind)
procedure: Choose concave or convex.
Move the object along the bench (u is negative).
Watch the three principal rays locate the image.
Read v, m and the nature of the image; record.
Cover all positions: beyond C, at C, between C and F, at F, between F and P — and the convex mirror (always virtual, diminished).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Mirror — Velocity of Image & Longitudinal Magnification
labs.aim: Move an object along the axis of a concave mirror and compare the speed of its image; show that v_image = −(v/u)² v_object = −m² v_object, while sideways motion is scaled by m.
labs.formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f      m = −v/u      Along axis: dv/dt = −(v²/u²) du/dt = −m² du/dt      Longitudinal magnification m_L = −m²      Perpendicular to axis: v_image = m × v_object      Newton: x₁ x₂ = f²
procedure: Set the object position u and its speed.
Choose motion along the axis or perpendicular to it.
Tap “Move” and compare object and image speeds.
Record at several positions.
Note: near F the image races away (m² large); at C both move at the same speed in opposite senses.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Refraction — Snell's Law, Critical Angle & Total Internal Reflection
labs.aim: Send a ray from one medium into another; verify n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, see bending towards / away from the normal, find the critical angle and observe total internal reflection.
labs.formula: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r      ₁n₂ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂ = sin i / sin r      Rarer → denser: bends towards the normal      Denser → rarer: bends away      Critical angle: sin c = n₂/n₁ (n₁ > n₂)      i > c → total internal reflection (no refracted ray)
procedure: Choose the two media.
Increase the angle of incidence i.
Record i and r; plot sin i against sin r — slope = n₂/n₁.
From a denser into a rarer medium, find the angle at which r = 90° (critical angle).
Go beyond it: all light reflects — total internal reflection.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Optical Fibre — Total Internal Reflection & Acceptance Angle
labs.aim: Send light into an optical fibre at different angles; see it trapped by repeated total internal reflection when the entry angle is within the acceptance angle, and leak out when it is not.
apparatus: Optical fibre: glass core (n₁) and cladding (n₂ < n₁)
labs.formula: At entry: sin θ = n₁ sin r      At the core–cladding wall the angle is (90° − r); TIR needs sin(90° − r) > n₂/n₁      Maximum acceptance angle: sin θ_max = √(n₁² − n₂²)  (numerical aperture)      Diamond sparkles because c ≈ 24° — light is trapped and reflected many times
procedure: Choose core and cladding.
Increase the entry angle θ from 0°.
Watch the zig-zag path: trapped (TIR) or leaking.
Record θ, the angle at the wall and whether TIR occurs.
Find the largest θ that is still trapped and compare with √(n₁² − n₂²).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Apparent Depth, Bird & Fish, and Normal Shift
labs.aim: Find how deep an object under water appears from above (near-normal viewing), work out what a bird sees of a fish and a fish sees of a bird, and measure the normal shift produced by a glass slab.
labs.formula: Viewed from the rarer medium: apparent depth = real depth / n,  shift = d (1 − 1/n)      Fish sees bird: apparent height = n H  (bird looks farther)      Bird sees fish: apparent depth = D / n  (fish looks nearer)      Glass slab of thickness t: normal shift = t (1 − 1/n)
procedure: Choose the situation.
Set the depths / heights and the liquid.
Read the apparent position and the shift.
Record.
Compare: the shift depends only on thickness and n, not on where the object is.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Refraction at a Single Curved Surface
labs.aim: Find the image formed by refraction at one spherical surface — a glass rod with a curved end, or a fish seen in a spherical bowl — using n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R.
apparatus: Glass rod with convex end (R = 10 cm)
labs.formula: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R   (light travels left → right; New Cartesian signs)      m = (n₁ v)/(n₂ u)      Focal lengths: f₁ = −n₁R/(n₂ − n₁),  f₂ = n₂R/(n₂ − n₁),  f₂/f₁ = −n₂/n₁
procedure: Choose the set-up.
Move the object (u is negative).
Read v, m and whether the image is real or virtual.
Record for several positions.
Fish bowl: the fish (at the centre) appears at the centre but magnified n times.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Thin Lenses — Ray Diagrams, Lens Formula & Lens Maker's Formula
labs.aim: Draw images by convex and concave lenses for every object position; verify 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u and the lens maker’s formula, and find the power in dioptres.
apparatus: Biconvex / biconcave lenses (choose R and n)
Object arrow on an optical bench
labs.formula: Lens maker: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)  → equi-convex: f = R / 2(n − 1)      Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f      m = v/u      Power P = 1/f (metre) dioptre: convex +, concave −      Convex: real & inverted beyond F, virtual & magnified within F;  concave: always virtual, erect, diminished
procedure: Choose the lens type, radius R and refractive index n — f is calculated by the lens maker’s formula.
Move the object along the bench.
Watch the two principal rays locate the image.
Record u, v, m and the nature of the image.
Change n: a lens of higher n is more powerful (shorter f).

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Focal Length by the Displacement Method
labs.aim: Keep the object and screen a fixed distance D apart and find the two lens positions that give a sharp image; get f = (D² − d²)/4D and the object size h = √(h₁h₂).
labs.formula: Sharp image is possible only if D ≥ 4f      Two positions separated by d:  f = (D² − d²) / (4D)      Image sizes h₁ (magnified) and h₂ (diminished):  h = √(h₁ h₂)
procedure: Set D (it must be at least 4f).
Slide the lens until the image on the screen is sharp — record.
Slide further to the second sharp position — record.
Calculate d, f and h from the two readings.
Reduce D below 4f: no sharp image can be found.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Power of Lenses — Combinations & Silvered Lens
labs.aim: Combine two thin lenses (in contact or separated) and find the equivalent power; then silver one face of a plano-convex lens and find the focal length of the resulting mirror.
apparatus: Plano-convex lens (R = 20 cm, n = 1.5) and silvering
labs.formula: P = 1/f (m) in dioptre      In contact: P = P₁ + P₂      Separated by d: P = P₁ + P₂ − d P₁ P₂      Silvered lens behaves as a mirror: P = 2P_lens + P_mirror  →  plane face silvered: F = f/2 = R/2(n − 1);  curved face silvered: F = R/2n
procedure: Choose the combination.
Set the lens powers (and separation).
Watch the parallel beam focus and read the equivalent power.
Record and check P = P₁ + P₂ (in contact).
Silvered lens: compare F for the plane face and the curved face silvered.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Human Eye — Myopia, Hypermetropia & Correction
labs.aim: See where the eye lens focuses light from near and far objects; find why a myopic eye cannot see far and a hypermetropic eye cannot see near, and calculate the power of the correcting lens.
apparatus: Model eye (retina 2.5 cm behind the lens)
labs.formula: Normal eye: near point 25 cm, far point ∞ (accommodation)      Myopia: far point F.P. < ∞ → image in front of the retina → concave lens, P = −100 / F.P.(cm)      Hypermetropia: near point N.P. > 25 cm → image behind the retina → convex lens, P = 100/25 − 100/N.P.(cm)      Presbyopia: both — bifocal lenses
procedure: Choose the eye.
Move the object from far to near.
See whether the rays meet on, in front of, or behind the retina.
Record the defect and the required lens power.
Switch on the corrective lens and check that the image falls on the retina.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Optical Instruments — Magnifier, Compound Microscope & Telescope
labs.aim: Find the magnifying power of a simple microscope, a compound microscope and an astronomical telescope, with the final image at the near point (D = 25 cm) or at infinity (normal adjustment).
apparatus: Convex lenses of different focal lengths
labs.formula: Simple microscope: M = 1 + D/f (image at D),  M = D/f (at ∞)      Compound microscope: M = (v₀/u₀)(1 + D/fₑ) at D;  M ≈ (L/f₀)(D/fₑ) at ∞      Telescope (normal adjustment): M = f₀/fₑ, tube length L = f₀ + fₑ;  image at D: M = (f₀/fₑ)(1 + fₑ/D)
procedure: Choose the instrument.
Set the focal lengths (and tube length).
Choose where the final image is formed.
Read the magnifying power and the length of the instrument; record.
Compare: a short-focus eyepiece and (for a telescope) a long-focus objective give a high magnification.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Physical Quantities, Units & Dimensional Analysis
labs.aim: Classify quantities as fundamental, derived or supplementary; find their SI, CGS and FPS units and dimensional formulae; check whether an equation is dimensionally correct; and derive the formula for the period of a pendulum by dimensions.
apparatus: Table of SI base quantities (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd)
Simple pendulum (length l, mass m) for the derivation
labs.formula: 7 SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd   ·   supplementary: rad, sr      Dimensional formula: [Mᵃ Lᵇ Tᶜ]      Principle of homogeneity: every term of a correct equation has the same dimensions      Pendulum: T = k lᵃ gᵇ mᶜ → [T] = [L]ᵃ[LT⁻²]ᵇ[M]ᶜ → c = 0, a = ½, b = −½  → T = k√(l/g)
procedure: Mode 1 — choose a quantity: read its type, units in SI/CGS/FPS and dimensional formula. Record.
Mode 2 — choose an equation and check every term: is it homogeneous?
Mode 3 — choose powers a, b, c for T = k lᵃ gᵇ mᶜ until the dimensions match [T].
Note: a dimensionally correct equation may still be wrong by a pure number (k = 2π).
Dimensionless quantities (angle, strain, refractive index) have formula [M⁰L⁰T⁰].

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Multiples, Prefixes & Unit Conversion
labs.aim: Use SI prefixes to write very large and very small quantities, convert units between systems with the dimensional method n₂ = n₁ [M₁/M₂]ᵃ[L₁/L₂]ᵇ[T₁/T₂]ᶜ, and meet practical units (light year, AU, parsec, ångström, fermi).
labs.formula: kilo 10³ · mega 10⁶ · giga 10⁹ · tera 10¹²  |  centi 10⁻² · milli 10⁻³ · micro 10⁻⁶ · nano 10⁻⁹ · pico 10⁻¹²      n₂ = n₁ (M₁/M₂)ᵃ (L₁/L₂)ᵇ (T₁/T₂)ᶜ  for [Mᵃ Lᵇ Tᶜ]      1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m · 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m · 1 pc = 3.26 ly · 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m · 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m
procedure: Mode 1 — set a value in metres with the exponent slider and read it with every prefix.
Choose the most convenient prefix (number between 1 and 1000).
Mode 2 — choose a conversion and follow the dimensional method step by step.
Record the result.
Check: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, 1 J = 10⁷ erg, 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Area of an Irregular Shape & Volume by Displacement
labs.aim: Estimate the area of a leaf on centimetre graph paper by counting squares (full = 1, half or more = 1, less than half = 0), and find the volume of an irregular stone from the rise of water in a measuring cylinder.
labs.formula: Area ≈ (number of full squares) + (number of squares at least half covered)  in cm²      Finer grid → better estimate      Volume of stone = V₂ − V₁ (water level after − before)      1 mL = 1 cm³
procedure: Mode 1 — choose the leaf and the grid size.
Count full squares and squares at least half covered (shown in colour).
Record the estimate and compare with the true area; use a finer grid.
Mode 2 — choose the stone and lower it into the cylinder.
Record V₁ and V₂; volume = V₂ − V₁.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Vectors — Triangle & Parallelogram Laws, Subtraction, Components
labs.aim: Add two vectors by the triangle and parallelogram laws, find the resultant’s magnitude and direction, subtract vectors, and resolve vectors into components.
apparatus: Two vectors A and B (displacements / forces)
labs.formula: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)      tan α = B sin θ / (A + B cos θ)  (angle of R with A)      |A − B| = √(A² + B² − 2AB cos θ)      Rmax = A + B (θ = 0°),  Rmin = |A − B| (θ = 180°)      Components: Ax = A cos φ, Ay = A sin φ;  R = (Ax + Bx) î + (Ay + By) ĵ
procedure: Set the magnitudes of A and B and the angle θ between them.
Choose triangle, parallelogram or subtraction.
Read R and its direction α; check by adding components.
Note the largest and smallest possible resultants.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Vector Products — Dot, Cross & Scalar Triple Product
labs.aim: Find the dot product (work = F·s) and cross product (torque, area) of two vectors as the angle between them changes; find the direction of A × B by the right-hand screw rule; and get the volume of a parallelepiped from the scalar triple product.
apparatus: Vectors A and B in the xy-plane
Vector C with a z-component (triple product)
labs.formula: A · B = AB cos θ  (scalar; zero when ⟂)      |A × B| = AB sin θ = area of parallelogram  (vector ⟂ to both; zero when ∥)      B × A = − A × B      A · (B × C) = volume of parallelepiped (zero if coplanar)      Work W = F · s,  torque τ = r × F,  L = r × p
procedure: Set |A|, |B| and the angle θ.
Read A · B and |A × B|; note when each is maximum or zero.
Choose “A × B” or “B × A” — the direction (out of / into the page) reverses.
Mode 3: set the height of C and read the triple-product volume.
Record and plot A·B and |A×B| against θ.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Equilibrium of Concurrent Forces — Lami's Theorem & Tangent Law
labs.aim: Hang a weight from two strings and measure the tensions; verify Lami’s theorem. Then push a hanging bob sideways with a horizontal force and verify the tangent law tan θ = F/W.
apparatus: Two strings with spring balances at adjustable angles
labs.formula: Lami: T₁ / sin α = T₂ / sin β = W / sin γ   (each force over the sine of the angle between the OTHER two)      Equilibrium: vector sum of forces = 0 (closed triangle)      Tangent law: tan θ = F / W,  T = √(W² + F²)
procedure: Choose Lami’s theorem or the tangent law.
Set the weight and the string angles (or the horizontal force).
Read the tensions on the spring balances.
Record and check that each T / sin(opposite angle) is the same.
Check the force triangle closes.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Wave Motion — Transverse & Longitudinal Waves, v = fλ
labs.aim: Watch particles of a medium as a wave passes: they only oscillate about their mean positions while energy travels. Compare transverse and longitudinal waves and verify v = f λ.
apparatus: Row of particles connected by springs (medium)
labs.formula: v = f λ      f = 1/T      Transverse: particles vibrate ⟂ to wave direction (crests & troughs) — e.g. string, light      Longitudinal: particles vibrate ∥ to wave direction (compressions & rarefactions) — e.g. sound      The medium does not travel with the wave; energy does
procedure: Choose the type of wave.
