Set the frequency f and the wave speed v (medium).
Measure the wavelength λ (crest to crest or compression to compression).
Record f, λ and v; check v = f λ.
Watch the red particle: it only moves to and fro.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Work Done — Positive, Zero & Negative; Work–Energy Theorem
labs.aim: Pull a block with a force at an angle and find the work done W = F s cos θ; see when work is positive, zero or negative; find the work done against gravity; and verify that net work equals the change in kinetic energy.
labs.formula: W = F · s = F s cos θ  (joule)      θ < 90°: positive · θ = 90°: zero · θ > 90°: negative      Lifting: W = m g h      Work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE = ½ m v² − ½ m u²      1 J = 10⁷ erg
procedure: Set the force F, its angle θ with the motion and the distance s.
Read the work done by F, by friction and by gravity.
Turn on friction: W_net = W_F − W_friction; compare with the KE gained.
Mode “lift”: work against gravity = mgh, independent of the path.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Power — Climbing Stairs & Lifting Loads
labs.aim: Measure your power by running up stairs (P = mgh/t), compare a slow and a fast lift, use P = F v for a moving vehicle, and convert between watt, horse power and kilowatt-hour.
apparatus: Motor lifting a load at constant speed
labs.formula: P = W / t = m g h / t      P = F v  (constant velocity)      1 W = 1 J/s      1 hp = 746 W      Energy (kWh) = P (kW) × t (h);  1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
procedure: Set your mass, the stair height and your time.
Tap “Climb” and read the power in W and hp.
Record and compare walking and running (same work, different power).
Mode “motor”: set force and speed; P = F v.
Find the energy (kWh) used if the motor runs for the given hours.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy — Roller Track
labs.aim: Release a ball on a smooth track and watch kinetic and potential energy change while their sum stays constant; add friction and see the “lost” energy appear as heat.
apparatus: Energy meters for KE, PE and heat
labs.formula: KE = ½ m v²      PE = m g h      Without friction: KE + PE = constant  →  v = √(2 g (h₀ − h))      With friction: KE + PE + heat = constant      Total energy is always conserved; it only changes form
procedure: Set the release height h₀ and friction.
Tap “Release” and watch the energy bars.
Pause at several points; record h, v, KE, PE.
Check KE + PE = m g h₀ (no friction).
With friction the ball never regains its starting height; the difference is heat.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Energy Transformations in Everyday Devices
labs.aim: Choose a device and see which form of energy goes in and which forms come out (energy flow diagram); find its efficiency and note that the total energy out always equals the energy in.
apparatus: Everyday devices: bulb, motor, generator, cell, solar cell, loudspeaker, microphone, heater, engine, plant, hydro plant
labs.formula: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed — only transformed      Energy in = sum of all energy out      Efficiency = useful energy out / energy in × 100 %      Forms: mechanical (KE, PE), heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical, nuclear
procedure: Choose a device and the input energy.
Read the energy flow: useful output and wasted output (mostly heat).
Record the efficiency.
Compare an LED with a filament bulb.
Check the outputs always add up to the input.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Springs — Elastic Potential Energy & Series / Parallel Combinations
labs.aim: Stretch springs singly, in series and in parallel; find the equivalent spring constant, the spring force F = −kx and the stored energy ½kx² as the area under the F–x graph.
labs.formula: F = − k x (restoring)      Work done in stretching = area under F–x = ½ k x² = elastic PE      Series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂  (softer)      Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂  (stiffer)      Spring force is conservative
procedure: Choose the arrangement and set k₁, k₂.
Set the extension x.
Read the force and the energy stored (shaded area).
Record and plot F against x: slope = equivalent k.
Compare series (smaller k) and parallel (larger k) for the same x.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Conservative & Non-conservative Forces — Path Independence
labs.aim: Move a block from A to B along different paths: the work done by gravity (and a spring) is the same for every path and zero round a closed loop, but the work done against friction depends on the path.
apparatus: Three paths from A to B: straight ramp, staircase, curved slide
labs.formula: Conservative force (gravity, spring, electrostatic): work depends only on start and end points; round trip work = 0; has a potential energy U, F = −dU/dx      Non-conservative (friction, air drag): work depends on path; round trip work ≠ 0 (energy lost as heat)      W_gravity = − m g Δh
procedure: Choose a path from A (top) to B (bottom).
Read the work done by gravity and by friction.
Record for all three paths.
Compare: gravity work is identical; friction work is greater for the longer path.
Choose “round trip” to go A → B → A: gravity gives zero net work, friction does not.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Potential-energy Curves & Types of Equilibrium
labs.aim: Place a ball on a potential-energy landscape U(x); find where the force F = −dU/dx is zero and decide whether each equilibrium is stable (U minimum), unstable (U maximum) or neutral (U constant).
labs.formula: F = − dU/dx      Equilibrium: F = 0 (dU/dx = 0)      Stable: U minimum (d²U/dx² > 0) — ball returns      Unstable: U maximum (d²U/dx² < 0) — ball moves away      Neutral: U constant — ball stays where placed
procedure: Choose the landscape.
Place the ball with the slider and read U and F = −dU/dx.
Find the points where F = 0.
Tap “Nudge” at each one: does the ball come back, run away or stay?
Record the type of equilibrium.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Power & Efficiency — Crane, Water Pump & the Heart
labs.aim: Find the useful (output) power of a crane, a water pump and the human heart, and compare it with the input power to get the efficiency.
apparatus: Pump lifting water to a tank
labs.formula: Efficiency η = output power / input power × 100 % = useful work / energy supplied      Crane: P_out = m g v  (= m g h / t)      Pump: P_out = (mass per second) g h = ρ Q g h  (+ ½ (dm/dt) v² if water leaves with speed v)      Heart: P = pressure × volume pumped per second
procedure: Choose the machine.
Set its load, rate and input power.
Read the output power and the efficiency.
Record and compare machines.
Check: η can never exceed 100 %.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Mass–Energy Equivalence — E = mc²
labs.aim: Convert a small mass into energy with E = mc² and compare it with everyday energies: lifting work, burning coal, a household’s electricity use, and the mass lost in nuclear fission.
labs.formula: E = m c²,  c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s      1 g of mass ≡ 9 × 10¹³ J      1 u (atomic mass unit) ≡ 931.5 MeV      In fission of U-235 about 0.1 % of the mass is converted to energy      Total (mass + energy) is conserved
procedure: Set the mass converted.
Read the energy E = mc².
Compare: how high could it lift a 1000 kg car? how much coal would release this? how long would it power a home?
Record for several masses.
Choose “fission” to see the mass defect of 1 kg of U-235.

labs.subject: physics
labs.title: Work–Energy Theorem — Bullet Penetration
labs.aim: Fire a bullet into a wooden block: the block’s constant resistive force does negative work equal to the bullet’s kinetic energy. Find how penetration depth depends on speed, and how many planks a bullet can pass through.
apparatus: Wooden block / identical planks (each 2 cm thick)
labs.formula: Work–energy theorem: − F s = 0 − ½ m u²  →  s = m u² / 2F      s ∝ u²: double the speed → 4× the depth      Through planks: each plank removes the same energy F d; speed after n planks v² = u² − 2 n F d / m      Time of penetration t = 2s/u
procedure: Set the bullet speed and the resistive force of the wood.
Choose a single block or a stack of planks.
Tap “Fire”. Read the penetration depth (or planks crossed).
Record for several speeds; plot s against u².
Check s = mu²/2F and t = 2s/u.
